awd_titl_txt: CAREER: Land-Use and Land-Cover Change Impact on Biodiversity and Indigenous Peoples' Livelihoods
awd_abstract_narration:
This CAREER award examines the drivers of fine-scale land-use and land-cover change and the impacts of these changes on biodiversity, ecosystem services and indigenous communities. Current methods to analyze biodiversity and ecosystem services use costly remotely sensed data at the spatial resolution of cities and urban centers that are not sufficient for analysis at a local scale. Working with Indigenous communities, this project develops novel remote sensing methods using Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) to collect data at finer spatial and temporal resolutions that enable the analysis of local land change processes while the changes are occurring. This project's use of co-production of knowledge of land-use and land-cover change identifies the processes that trigger land-use change and thereby makes a significant contribution to research on scaling up methods that inform sustainable global economic processes. The tightly integrated research and education plans coupled with a summer institute broaden participation of underrepresented students and provides exceptional training in STEM research methods. 

As land change scientists extend models for understanding the implications of change processes, it is essential to know how, when, and where the impacts of global level processes are manifested at local scales. To address these needs, this project catalogs change occurring at the local level using geospatial information technologies, including drones, and evaluates what forces drive change at the local level. Evaluation of local change processes will be completed in five different physical environments to determine whether and how policymakers respond to global-level drivers of change. This research fills a gap in the understanding of how local-level biodiversity, ecosystem services availability, and indigenous peoples' livelihood practices are shaped by forces located far from urban centers.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
This project examined the drivers and implications of fine-scale land-use and land-cover change processes on human populations, biodiversity, and ecosystem services within indigenous peoples influenced landscapes of Guyana, South America. Working in five titled indigenous Amerindian Villages, with local indigenous peoples’ collaborators, the project obtained data from drones, camera traps, qualitative survey instruments, and observations for wildlife and signs of wildlife. The project established four (4) 5-km long transects in each village that became the basis for understanding the ways in which indigenous peoples shaped landscapes, including determining the distribution of ecosystem services. The project obtained data that provided insights into the ways indigenous peoples cultural practices are changing relative to larger societal pressures emanating from beyond village boundaries, including on the types of crops that are grown, in addition to how larger processes such as changes in climatic and weather conditions drive changes in cultural practices. Through the utility of drone data and field sampling by local people, databases on the distribution of swidden plots were developed for each village, along with the types of crops that are cultivated within each village. The data showed that the density and distribution of wildlife is closely connected to the location of farms in each village, as are the location and distribution of trees and palms that are associated with important ecosystem services for indigenous peoples. The analysis found that in villages with stronger connections to the cultivation of the traditional staple cassava crop (Manihot esculenta), there was a higher density of wildlife, including the presence of herbivores that support both human and larger apex predator populations, as opposed to those villages where cassava was absent or cultivated. Drone data were successfully used to identify and map the cassava crop within the context of swidden agriculture landscapes.

 

This project developed a first-of-its-kind approach to obtaining imagery using drones where local people were actively involved and frequently led data collection campaigns. The project has developed a strong sense of the distribution of past and current swidden agriculture plots within the five study villages and has developed the tools to model how future farm development in the villages may affect the density and distribution of wildlife and ecosystem services that are critical to the livelihoods of indigenous peoples. Five Ph.D. dissertations were developed across the project, an addressed 1) the identification and distribution of palms species relative to swidden agriculture plots, 2) the identification of swidden agriculture plots in Guyana and globally through remotely sensed data, 3) assessing the distribution of herbivores and their related carnivores relative to the distribution of farms, 4) identifying the cassava crops from drone imagery using machine learning methods, and 5) mapping the distribution of crime in Guyana and understanding the implications for spill over to swidden landscapes. Overall, ten papers were published in peer-reviewed journals from the data, analysis and efforts associated with the project over its lifetime. An estimated additional fifteen papers will be published in scientific journals based on the data and knowledge created through this project.

 

The project relied on human-centered methods for obtaining data on the ways in which indigenous people shape their swidden landscapes. Throughout the course of the project, ten American undergraduate students traveled to Guyana to participate in the Summer Field Institute (SFI) in 2022 and 2024. The groups that traveled in 2022 interacted with students from the Bina Hill Institute (BHI) primarily Makushi young people, who accompanied them in completing interviews and surveys of residents of five Rupununi villages on their perceptions on changes in climatic and land-use realities on cultural practices. The 2022 and 2024 groups (five and 4 persons, respectively), were provided introductions to the Makushi language by a local teacher and spent time learning about the swidden agriculture process in the Rupununi. The one student who traveled to Guyana in summer 2023 learned about the processes of collecting data using drones. Overall, the project supported the dissertation project of five (5) Ph.D. students, the capstone projects of three (3) master’s students, and the senior research project of two undergraduates at the University of Texas at Dallas. Two of the undergraduates who attended the 2022 SFI have gone on to graduate school at Wesleyan University. At least two persons in each were trained to fly drones and have been licensed by the Guyana Civil Aviation Authority (GCAA) to fly drones in Guyana after they were prepared by the project. Through the project and related work, the PI’s career is poised to make important contributions to the geospatial information sciences body of knowledge, and his profile as a researcher on human-wildlife interactions has been significantly enhanced.
